name: Ketogenic diet
short: Child epilepsy: deaths (case reports: low selenium with cardiomyopathy or long QT; pancreatitis); severe events ≤0.5%; kidney stones 5.8%. Autism: scurvy (case); trial: 18 of 47 stopped (adherence).
text: Most data come from children with epilepsy on the classic or medium-chain triglyceride diet; the autism page's diet is a modified ketogenic diet, and the 62-child autism trial abstract reports no adverse-event data. In a 2026 randomised trial in children with autism (47 on a ketogenic diet, 30 controls, for three months), most adverse events were mild, and 18 of the 47 stopped the diet after one month, which the authors take to indicate adherence challenges (the abstract does not say whether adverse events contributed). In a randomised trial in 160 people aged 10 to 55 with drug-resistant epilepsy (80 adults and 80 adolescents) of the modified Atkins diet added to standard medicines, against standard medicines alone, one patient had weight loss and two had diarrhoea (the abstract does not say in which group, or describe the diet's make-up). Serious harms: in a systematic review of 45 prospective studies in children with refractory epilepsy, severe adverse events such as respiratory failure and pancreatitis occurred in no more than 0.5% of children, and none of the 24 deaths reported after starting the diet was attributed to it; the most common adverse events were gut disturbances (40.6%), raised blood fats (12.8%), raised uric acid (4.4%), lethargy (4.1%), infections (3.8%) and low blood protein (3.8%). On the other side, case reports describe deaths in children on the diet: two children on it for seizure control, both with selenium deficiency, died, one of a heart rhythm disturbance (torsade de pointes) with QT prolongation, with selenium-deficiency heart muscle disease (cardiomyopathy) found after death, and one suddenly at home after QT prolongation; and a 9-year-old girl with a seizure disorder from glucose transporter deficiency, on the medium-chain triglyceride diet since infancy, died of acute pancreatitis, with haemorrhagic pancreatitis confirmed after death. In a retrospective Korean multicentre series of 199 infants, children and adolescents with refractory epilepsy, five died during the diet (the abstract does not give the causes). At one centre, nine patients on the diet had low selenium, one of whom developed cardiomyopathy (the other eight, found on screening, had normal heart evaluations), and selenium was low in 20% of the patients evaluated (children already on or starting the diet were screened). A review of children and infants with epilepsy lists vomiting, low blood sugar, metabolic acidosis and refusal of the diet as common when it is started, and pancreatitis, protein-losing enteropathy, prolonged QT interval, cardiomyopathy and changes in the basal ganglia as rare and serious. Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), which the authors call a rarely reported but potentially fatal adverse effect, developed in a 5-year-old with autism from the diet's restrictions (a case report); a 16-year-old who lost one hundred pounds while following a 'ketogenic' diet developed Wernicke's encephalopathy, a thiamine deficiency (a case report). Bones, calcium and kidneys: in 25 children with intractable epilepsy on the diet for 15 months, whole-body and spine bone mineral content-for-age fell by 0.6 z score a year and height by 0.5 z score a year, with suboptimal blood vitamin D and calcium and vitamin D intake; in a multicentre case series, 14 children (aged 0.9 to 18) developed high blood calcium 0.2 to 12 years after starting the diet, half of them with impaired kidney function at presentation. A meta-analysis of 36 studies estimated a kidney stone incidence of 5.8% in children on ketogenic diets. Growth: in 237 children (aged 2 months to 9 years) with intractable epilepsy, weight scores dropped quickly in the first 3 months and height scores changed more by 2 years, and the authors say the diet generally provides enough nutrition to maintain growth within normal limits over a defined period but that very young children grow poorly on it; in 63 infants under 12 months, growth velocity did not fall in the first year but fell in the second year in those still on the diet. A 2023 review says strict evaluation of growth and nutritional status is essential in long-term use. Medicines: in a chart review of 93 children, 6 had confirmed kidney stones, 3 of them among 17 children also taking zonisamide and 1 among 22 also taking topiramate (anti-seizure medicines that inhibit carbonic anhydrase), and all 6 had biochemical risk factors that included metabolic acidosis; in 14 children taking topiramate with the diet, bicarbonate fell considerably in most, mainly when the diet was started, 2 needed bicarbonate supplements to continue it, and none had kidney stones.
